title: Forms
bridge: On the web, input comes from **forms**: `<input>`, `<select>`, `<textarea>` and a `<button>`, each with a `<label>`. The browser can check simple things itself (`required`, `type="number"`, `min`), and JavaScript reads the values later in the course.
lesson:
Forms are how a page asks for information.

```
<form>
  <label for="crop">Crop</label>
  <select id="crop" name="crop" required>
    <option>maize</option>
    <option>beans</option>
  </select>

  <label for="kg">Weight (kg)</label>
  <input id="kg" name="kg" type="number" min="0" step="0.1" required>

  <label for="day">Date</label>
  <input id="day" name="day" type="date">

  <button type="submit">Save</button>
</form>
```

- **Every input needs a label**, joined by `for` matching the input's `id`. Clicking the label focuses the box (a bigger target on a phone), and screen readers read the label out.
- `type` changes the keyboard on phones and what's allowed: `number`, `date`, `email`, `tel`, `password`, `checkbox`.
- The browser checks `required`, `min`, `max` and `maxlength` before sending, for free.
- `name` is the key the value is sent under; `<textarea>` is for longer text; `<select>` for a fixed choice.

Good forms ask for as little as possible, say exactly what's wrong, and never throw away what someone typed.

notes: Each label's for matches an id.
A number box that can't go below 0.

exercises.title: A sign-up form
exercises.prompt: Make a form with labelled inputs for name (text, required), phone (type tel), age (number, min 5, max 120) and a submit button. Every input must have an id and a label whose for matches it.

hints: Phone: type="tel"; age: type="number" min="5" max="120".
